uses.text: Building construction is the largest use (42 %).
Electrical and electronic products (23 %); cables and wiring are its key application.
Transport equipment (18 %), consumer goods (10 %) and industrial machinery (7 %).

hazardStatements.text: Very toxic to aquatic life with long lasting effects

hazards.note: EU harmonised classification (CLP Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008, Annex VI), via PubChem.

crust.note: Earth's crust, as given (mg/kg is parts per million by mass).

ocean.note: Sea water, mg/L read as mg/kg: a litre of sea water is taken as one kilogram (it is slightly heavier; the difference cannot be seen on a logarithmic scale).

body.note: Grams in the 70 kg reference adult of ICRP Publication 23, divided by its mass.

origin.note: Read off Fig. 39 at the dotted 'age of the Sun' line (t = 9.2 Gyr after the Big Bang, 4.6 Gyr ago): pixel fractions of the stacked areas (agb 0.139, massive_stars 0.854, neutron_star_mergers 0.001, white_dwarfs 0.006); quantised to 0.05. Stack height 62 px. Paper: 'For the elements from Ne to Ge, the newly synthesized amounts are very small for AGB stars, and the small green areas are mostly for mass loss.'

air.text: Dulls slowly in air and, in moist air, gathers the green coat of basic carbonate seen on copper roofs; heating gives a black oxide.

water.text: Insoluble in water and not attacked by it.

acids.text: Hardly attacked by cold hydrochloric or dilute sulfuric acid, but readily by dilute nitric acid and hot concentrated sulfuric acid.

splitting.note: Atomic-beam microwave measurement (Ting and Lew 1957), as quoted in arXiv:2210.11425. A derived as splitting/2.
Atomic-beam microwave measurement (Ting and Lew 1957), as quoted in arXiv:2210.11425; the same A appears as the reference value in arXiv:1011.5420.

plantRole.text: Carries electrons in plastocyanin of photosynthesis and in cytochrome c oxidase; also needed for lignin and pollen formation.

humanRole.text: Part of cytochrome c oxidase, superoxide dismutase and the proteins that handle iron.

roles.text: Needed by enzymes of respiration, iron transport, pigment and connective tissue; lambs of copper-deficient ewes can be born with swayback.
Some molluscs and arthropods carry oxygen in their blood with haemocyanin, in which a pair of copper atoms binds each oxygen molecule.
Yeast needs it in cytochrome c oxidase for respiration, in copper–zinc superoxide dismutase and in the oxidase Fet3 that takes up iron.
About seven in ten sequenced bacteria use it, mostly those that live with oxygen, above all in cytochrome c oxidase; most anaerobes have no copper proteins.
Only about a third of the sequenced archaea use it, all of them in cytochrome c oxidase, the enzyme that hands electrons to oxygen.

uptake.text: Cu²⁺; when copper is scarce, roots first reduce it to Cu⁺

known.by: C. B. Lipman and G. MacKinney

deficiency.text: Young leaves are distorted and bleached, and stems bend or twist because their walls lack lignin, so cereals fall over (lodge) easily. Grain and fruit suffer most, because copper-short plants make sterile pollen.
Cereals turn bushy, with white twisted leaf tips and partly empty ears. Oats, spinach, wheat and lucerne respond most to copper fertiliser; beans, grass, potatoes and soybeans least.

toxicity.text: Copper builds up in soils from years of copper fungicides (in vineyards and coffee plantations), sewage sludge and pig or poultry slurry. Roots stop growing first, because they trap most of the excess.

soil.text: Shortage occurs on soils naturally poor in copper, such as leached sandy soils, and on soils that bind it, such as peats, limy and some clay soils; it is common enough on newly drained peat to be called 'reclamation disease'.
Copper sulfate or oxide spread on the soil can keep working for decades, up to 30 years in southern Australia; leaf sprays act faster but can scorch leaves if too strong.

partners.text: Plants with arbuscular mycorrhiza usually take up more copper and zinc than plants without the fungus.
Too much copper in the soil harms nitrogen fixation in legume nodules.

wild.text: On the copper-rich soils of the Democratic Republic of Congo grow copper-tolerant plants whose leaves have been reported to hold around 1,000 mg per kg of dry matter, though some of this may be dust on the leaves.
Common bent grass on the spoil of a Welsh copper mine evolved copper-tolerant populations within about a century, very fast by the usual pace of evolution.

forest.text: Twisted, deformed leading shoots in Douglas-fir have been traced to copper shortage, and in some cases to boron shortage.

food.text: Copper fertilisers can raise copper in food and fodder where people or livestock lack it, but must be used with care, because too much harms plants and animals.
Sheep are especially sensitive to copper-rich fodder; about 50 mg per kg of dry matter is taken as the upper limit for forage.

levels.part: leaves from the base of new shoots

levels.note: Possible deficiency below this level (Carter 1992, cited in chapter 13); the book says micronutrient critical levels in trees are not well established.

history.nameOrigin: From the Latin cuprum, from aes Cyprium, 'metal of Cyprus', the Romans' main source.
history.symbolNote: Cu comes from the Latin cuprum.

prose.text: Copper is a soft, reddish metal that conducts electricity better than any other except silver, which is why it runs through our walls as wiring; alloyed with tin it gave the Bronze Age its name, and with zinc it becomes brass. Plants need traces of it too, for plastocyanin, a small copper protein that ferries electrons in photosynthesis. Copper breaks the simple filling rule: the Aufbau order predicts [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s², but measurement shows [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, a completely filled d subshell plus one s electron (ground term ²S₁/₂). In the metal, those d electrons absorb blue and green light, leaving copper its warm colour.
